title: Play until you win
summary: Repeat the game with loop, stop with break, and replace the crash on bad input with a second chance. Then build the game's logic yourself, checked by real tests.

sections: TRPL 2 Allowing Multiple Guesses with Looping
TRPL 2 Quitting After a Correct Guess
PR ch2 Writing and Running Unit Tests

blocks.md: The game so far allows exactly one guess. In this lesson you make it repeat until the player wins, stop cleanly, and survive input like `foo` without crashing. Then you write the game's logic yourself as small functions, and Rust's test runner tells you when they are right.

blocks.title: loop and break
blocks.md: `loop` repeats a block of code **forever**: when the end of the block is reached, it starts again at the top. To get out, use `break`, which ends the loop immediately. In the game we break when the guess is correct. Because `match` arms can hold several statements inside `{ }`, the `Equal` arm can both print and break:

blocks.title: A second chance instead of a crash
blocks.md: With `.expect`, typing `foo` still crashes the whole game. We want to ignore the bad line and ask again. Since `parse` returns a `Result`, we can `match` on it just like on `Ordering`:

blocks.explain:
- If parsing worked, the value is `Ok(num)`. The pattern `Ok(num)` **binds** the number inside to the name `num`, and the arm's result is `num`. That becomes the value of the whole `match`, which is stored in `guess`.
- If parsing failed, the value is `Err(...)`. The `_` is a **catch-all**: it matches any error, and we don't care which. `continue` jumps straight to the next round of the `loop`, so the game asks for another guess.

Moving from `expect` to `match` is the usual path in Rust: crash while you are sketching, then handle the error properly.

blocks.title: Splitting logic out so it can be tested
blocks.md:
Real Rust projects keep their logic in small **functions** that take values and return results, and leave reading the keyboard to `main`. Functions like that can be checked automatically by **unit tests**: small functions marked `#[test]` that call your code and check the result with `assert_eq!(actual, expected)`. `cargo test` finds and runs them all.

*Programming Rust* shows this right after its `gcd` function:

blocks.explain: `#[test]` is an **attribute**: a note to the compiler. It marks `test_gcd` as a test, so it is compiled and run by `cargo test` and left out of a normal build. If an `assert_eq!` sees two different values, the test fails and shows both. You will write tests yourself in chapter 11; for now you will *use* them to check your exercises.

blocks.title: How the exercises below work
blocks.md:
Press **Open in console**, write your code in `src/lib.rs`, and press **Run tests**. The tests in `src/tests.rs` are read-only; open that tab to see exactly what is checked. Each test turns green when your function returns the right value. With `start.sh` running, your edits are also saved into `exercises/<folder>/src/lib.rs`, so you can work in your own editor and run `cargo test` there.

`todo!()` in the starter code is a placeholder that panics when reached. Replace it with your code.

blocks.title: Too small, too big, you win
blocks.goal: Write the function at the heart of the game: given a guess and the secret, return the message the game prints.
blocks.behavior:
`pub fn verdict(guess: u32, secret: u32) -> &'static str` returns:

- `"Too small!"` when `guess` is less than `secret`
- `"Too big!"` when `guess` is greater than `secret`
- `"You win!"` when they are equal

(`&'static str` is the type of a piece of fixed text written in quotes in your program. Chapter 4 explains the `&` and chapter 10 the `'static`.)
hints: Start with `use std::cmp::Ordering;` at the top of the file.
`match guess.cmp(&secret) { ... }` with three arms; each arm's result is the text, with no `println!` and no semicolon.
A function returns the value of its last expression, so the `match` itself can be the last thing in the function.
blocks.solution_explain: The `match` is the last expression of the function, so its value is returned. Each arm produces a piece of text instead of printing it, which is what makes the function testable.

blocks.title: Read a guess safely
blocks.goal: Turn a line typed by the player into a guess, without ever crashing on bad input.
blocks.behavior:
`pub fn parse_guess(line: &str) -> Option<u32>` returns:

- `Some(n)` when the line, after removing surrounding spaces and the newline, is a whole number `n` from **1 to 100**
- `None` for anything else: text, an empty line, negative numbers, 0, or numbers above 100

**Option** is a close cousin of Result for "maybe there is a value": it is either `Some(value)` or `None`. Chapter 6 covers it fully.
hints: `match line.trim().parse::<u32>() { Ok(n) => ..., Err(_) => None }`. The `::<u32>` tells `parse` the target type without a `let` annotation.
Inside the `Ok(n)` arm, check the range: `if n >= 1 && n <= 100 { Some(n) } else { None }`. In Rust, `if` produces a value too.
Parsing `"-5"` as `u32` already fails, so negative numbers land in the `Err` arm by themselves.
blocks.solution_explain: `trim` handles spaces and both kinds of newline. `parse::<u32>()` rejects text and negative numbers by returning `Err`. The `if` inside the `Ok` arm rejects numbers outside the game's range. (Later you will learn shorter ways to write this, such as `.ok()` and `.filter(...)`.)

blocks.title: The whole game, as a function
blocks.goal: Combine the two previous exercises into the complete game: given the secret and the lines the player typed, produce exactly what the game prints.
blocks.behavior:
`pub fn play(secret: u32, lines: &[&str]) -> Vec<String>` goes through `lines` in order and builds the list of messages the game would print:

- For a line that is not a valid guess (use the rules of `parse_guess`): add `"Please type a number!"` and go on to the next line.
- For a valid guess `n`: add `"You guessed: n"`, then the verdict (`"Too small!"`, `"Too big!"` or `"You win!"`).
- After `"You win!"`, stop: later lines are ignored.
- If the lines run out before a win, just return what you have.

`&[&str]` is a list of text lines, and `Vec<String>` is a growable list of Strings. The starter already creates the list and returns it; you only add to it with `output.push(...)`. `format!` works like `println!` but gives back a String instead of printing it.

examples.output: ["You guessed: 10", "Too small!", "You guessed: 80", "Too big!", "You guessed: 61", "You win!"]

hints: Copy your `verdict` and `parse_guess` functions into this file. Splitting work into functions you already trust is half the job.
`for line in lines { ... }` visits every line. Use `match parse_guess(line) { Some(n) => ..., None => ... }`.
`output.push(format!("You guessed: {n}"));` and `output.push(verdict(n, secret).to_string());` (`to_string` turns fixed text into a String).
After pushing the verdict, `if n == secret { break; }`.
blocks.solution_explain: The solution reuses the two earlier functions. `parse_guess` uses a **match guard** (`Ok(n) if ...`), a pattern with an extra condition, which chapter 19 covers; the `if` version from the previous exercise works just as well.

blocks.title: Bonus: reading command-line arguments
blocks.md: *Programming Rust* ends its first program by reading numbers from the **command line**, the words typed after the program's name. `std::env::args()` gives them as Strings; the first one is the program's own name, so `.skip(1)` drops it. You will build a full command-line tool in chapter 12.

blocks.explain: `cargo run -- 4 8 15`: everything after `--` is passed to your program instead of to Cargo.

options: Skips the rest of this round and starts the next one
questions.explanation: `continue` jumps to the start of the next round; `break` leaves the loop.

questions.explanation: `_` is a catch-all pattern that ignores the value.

questions.q: Without a `break`, a `loop` runs until the program is stopped from outside.
questions.explanation: `loop` repeats forever by design (or until a `break`, a `return`, or a panic).

questions.q: The player types `abc`. Which version of the game keeps running?
options: `let guess: u32 = guess.trim().parse().expect("Please type a number!");`
`let guess: u32 = match guess.trim().parse() { Ok(num) => num, Err(_) => continue };`
questions.explanation: `expect` panics on `Err`, ending the program. The `match` version continues the loop.
`n` goes 1, 2, 3; at 3 the loop breaks and 3 is printed.

points: `loop { ... }` repeats forever; `break` leaves it, `continue` starts the next round.
A `match` arm can run several statements inside `{ }`.
`match value.parse() { Ok(num) => num, Err(_) => continue }` handles bad input instead of panicking.
`Ok(num)` binds the inner value to `num`; `_` matches anything and ignores it.
Logic in small functions that return values can be checked with unit tests (`#[test]`, `assert_eq!`, `cargo test`).
`std::env::args()` gives the command-line arguments as Strings.

terms.def: Repeats its block forever, until `break` (or `return`) leaves it.
Skips the rest of the current round of a loop and starts the next one.
A small function marked `#[test]` that calls your code and checks the result; `cargo test` runs them all.
A value that is either `Some(value)` or `None`: Rust's way of saying 'there may be no value' without null.
A growable list of values of one type, like `Vec<String>`.
